correctness.rationale: The complete lost-ballot polynomial follows from independent cycle-abstention and disjoint rooted off-cycle subtrees. Every bound is proved for arbitrary finite loopless functional graphs using cycle length ≥2; sharp equality graphs and the six-voter tail reversal follow algebraically. The self-contained checker separately enumerates every casting set in 2,534 graph cases and checks 33,478 graph-and-probability bound cases with exact rational arithmetic. Finite tests are auxiliary.

originality.rationale: The fully inspected 2026 default-delegation primary source derives expectations and a Hamiltonian-cycle minimum, but it does not supply the complete loss-count generating polynomial, the sharp maximizing graph/equality laws, or the strict reversal between expected and high-tail loss. Expected voting weight/centrality addresses a distinct first-moment quantity. Exact equivalence searches found no covering public record, with explicitly retained residual risk of unindexed/alternative reliability formulations.
residual_risks: Unindexed network reliability or branching-process work might contain an equivalent probability generating function after translation to default delegation.
Brill et al. already give first moments and the minimizing topology; maximizing the mean is a short new optimization of known expectations and not itself the central novel technical ingredient.

Full primary mathematical text of Grossi et al. was not reliably fetched in the latest access attempt, although its abstract and detailed accounts specify a different first-moment centrality objective.
A targeted semantic search cannot establish universal originality; a specialist literature audit remains unperformed.

value.rationale: Exact probabilities of losing any or at least k ballots and the existence of incompatible risk orderings are essential reliability questions for liquid democracy, not recoverable from an expected-loss value alone. Sharp extremizers/equality and a strict mean–tail inversion distinguish design objectives and provide natural interpretive and computational benchmarks for probabilistic delegation networks.
